intro-ecosystems: An ecosystem joins a community of species to the abiotic conditions around it. Species interact by predation (+/−), competition (−/−) and three kinds of symbiosis: mutualism (+/+), commensalism (+/0) and parasitism (+/−). Species that need the same resource can still coexist by resource partitioning, using it at different places or times.
terrestrial-biomes: Terrestrial biomes are set mainly by temperature and precipitation. Tundra and taiga are cold; grassland, chaparral, deciduous forest and temperate rainforest are temperate; desert, savanna and tropical rainforest are warm. A climatograph shows monthly temperature and precipitation, so you can read a biome off it. Savannas are not deserts: they have a wet season and a dry season.
aquatic-biomes: Aquatic biomes differ mainly in salinity, depth, light, temperature and dissolved oxygen. Freshwater biomes include lakes (with littoral, limnetic, profundal and benthic zones), rivers and wetlands; marine biomes include estuaries, the intertidal zone, coral reefs and the open ocean. Plants and algae need the photic zone, and colder, moving water holds more oxygen.
math-sci-notation: Scientific notation writes very large and very small numbers as a number from 1 to 10 times a power of ten, such as 2.5×10⁶ = 2.5 million = 2,500,000. To multiply, multiply the fronts and add the exponents; to divide, divide and subtract. Metric prefixes (kilo, mega, giga, milli, micro) are powers of ten too, so change them before you compare or combine numbers.
carbon-cycle: Carbon cycles among the atmosphere, living things, soil, the ocean, sediments and rock, and fossil fuels. Photosynthesis removes CO2 from the air; respiration, decomposition and combustion return it. The ocean and growing forests act as carbon sinks. Burning fossil fuels moves slow-cycle carbon into the air far faster than sinks remove it, so atmospheric CO2 rises.
nitrogen-cycle: Nitrogen’s largest reservoir is N2 gas in the air, which most organisms cannot use. Bacteria fix it into ammonium, nitrifying bacteria turn ammonium into nitrate, plants assimilate nitrate, decomposers return ammonium by ammonification, and denitrifying bacteria in low-oxygen soil return N2 to the air. Nitrogen often limits plant growth, and excess fertilizer nitrate leaches into water.
phosphorus-cycle: Phosphorus is stored mostly in rock and ocean sediments and has no significant gas phase, so it cycles slowly. Weathering releases phosphate, plants take it up, animals eat plants, and decomposers return it to the soil. Rain carries phosphate on soil into water, where it settles as sediment. Phosphorus often limits growth in fresh water, so extra phosphate makes algae grow.
water-cycle: The water cycle moves water among the ocean, air, land, ice and groundwater. The sun drives evaporation and transpiration; vapor condenses into clouds and falls as precipitation; on land it runs off to rivers or infiltrates to recharge aquifers. Almost all water is salty ocean water, and most freshwater is ice or groundwater. Paving increases runoff and reduces recharge.
math-rates: A rate divides one quantity by another: liters per day, people per km², kilograms per person. A per-capita value divides a total by the number of people, so places of different sizes can be compared fairly. Write the setup with units: the word after "per" goes on the bottom, and the units of the answer tell you what you found.
math-units: Dimensional analysis converts units by multiplying by conversion factors, fractions equal to 1, arranged so unwanted units cancel. Write every factor with units in the setup, then the answer with its unit. Power (watts, kW) is a rate; energy (kWh, J, BTU, kcal) is an amount, and energy = power × time. Cost and emissions follow the same pattern: kWh × price per kWh, kWh × kg CO2 per kWh.
primary-productivity: Primary productivity is the rate at which producers capture energy by photosynthesis. Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total; producers use part of it in respiration (R); the rest, net primary productivity, NPP = GPP - R, becomes plant matter that animals can eat. Productivity is highest where light, water, warmth and nutrients are all plentiful.
trophic-levels: Trophic levels sort organisms by how they get energy. Producers (level 1) make food from light; primary consumers (herbivores, level 2) eat producers; secondary and tertiary consumers eat the levels below; an apex predator is at the top. Omnivores feed at more than one level. Arrows point from food to eater, so a change at one level ripples to the others.
math-percents: A percent is a part out of 100: part ÷ whole × 100. Percent of a quantity is (percent ÷ 100) × quantity. Percent change is (new - old) / old × 100: subtract inside brackets, divide by the starting value, multiply by 100, and keep the sign. Show this setup exactly; readers give a point for it.
energy-flow: Energy enters ecosystems through producers and flows one way, up the trophic levels. At each step about 90% is used for life processes and lost as heat, so only about 10% passes on: multiply by 0.10 for each step. This explains energy pyramids, the small number of trophic levels and why eating at a lower level feeds more people. Energy is not destroyed; it leaves as heat.
food-webs: A food chain follows one path of energy from producers to top consumers; a food web shows all the overlapping chains in an ecosystem. Arrows point from food to eater. Decomposers and detritivores recycle nutrients from every level. Because organisms are linked, a change in one population spreads: prey increase when predators decline, and the effect can reach plants several links away.
biodiversity: Biodiversity is variety at three levels: genes within a population, species within a community, and habitats within an area. Species diversity combines richness (how many species) and evenness (how equal they are). More diverse populations and ecosystems usually recover better from stress, a bottleneck leaves a population with little genetic diversity, and a keystone species holds its community together.
ecosystem-services: Ecosystem services are the benefits people get from working ecosystems: provisioning (goods such as food, timber and water), regulating (pollination, water purification, flood control, carbon storage), cultural (recreation, tourism, beauty) and supporting (photosynthesis, nutrient cycling, soil building). Damaging an ecosystem removes services that then cost money to replace.
island-biogeo: Island biogeography explains species richness on islands: larger islands hold more species because fewer species die out there, and islands nearer the mainland hold more because more colonists arrive. The same rules apply to habitat fragments, which act like islands, so breaking up a habitat into small, isolated patches lowers the number of species it can keep.
ecological-tolerance: Every species has a range of tolerance for each abiotic factor. In the optimal range individuals thrive and populations are largest; in the zones of physiological stress they survive but grow and reproduce poorly; beyond the limits, in the zones of intolerance, they die. Where conditions move out of a species’ range, its population shrinks, moves or disappears.
natural-disruptions: Natural disruptions such as floods, droughts, fires, storms and eruptions change ecosystems for a short or a long time. They can be periodic (regular), episodic (recurring at irregular intervals) or random. Over geological time, Earth’s climate and sea level have changed many times. Organisms respond by surviving in place, migrating to suitable places, or dying out locally.
evolving-populations: Populations respond to environmental change through natural selection. Individuals differ in heritable traits; those whose traits suit the environment survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common over generations, and the population becomes adapted. Individuals do not adapt within their lifetime, and populations with little genetic variety, or facing very fast change, may not adapt in time.
succession: Ecological succession is the series of changes in a community after a disruption. Primary succession begins on bare rock with no soil, and pioneer species such as lichens and mosses help form soil; it is slow. Secondary succession begins where soil remains, after a fire, flood or abandoned farm; it is faster. Over the stages, biodiversity and biomass increase until a mature, more stable climax community develops.
generalists-specialists: Specialist species have narrow niches: a few foods, one habitat or a narrow range of conditions. They thrive where their resource is stable but decline when the environment changes. Generalist species have broad niches and can switch foods and habitats, so they cope better with change and often spread into new and disturbed places.
r-k-selection: r-selected species have many small offspring, little parental care, early reproduction and short lives; they have a high biotic potential, their populations swing up and down, and they rebound quickly after a disruption. K-selected species have few large offspring, much parental care, late reproduction and long lives; their populations are steadier but recover slowly from losses. Most species fall between the two ends.
survivorship-curves: A survivorship curve plots the number of survivors from a group born at the same time against age. Type I curves stay high and drop in old age, Type II curves fall steadily (a straight line on a log scale), and Type III curves drop steeply early in life. Survivorship describes when deaths happen; it is related to, but not the same as, r- and K-selection, which describe how a species reproduces.
carrying-limits: Carrying capacity is the largest population an environment can support over time. A population that grows past it is in overshoot and uses resources faster than they are replaced; resource shortages then cause dieback, a sharp population crash. Because overshoot can damage the resources, carrying capacity may be lower afterward than before.
math-doubling: A population growing by a fixed percent each year doubles in a fixed time. By the rule of 70, doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate in percent. Add the doubling time to the start year for "in what year"; multiply by 2 for each doubling to project the size. Doubling time depends only on the rate: twice the rate, half the time.
population-growth: With unlimited resources, a population grows exponentially (a J-curve), by a constant percent each period. In real environments, limiting factors slow growth as the population nears carrying capacity, giving logistic growth (an S-curve). Density-dependent factors such as food shortage, disease and competition strengthen as a population grows; density-independent factors such as floods and frosts act whatever its size.
age-structure: An age structure diagram shows a population’s size by age group and sex, each bar a cohort. A wide base (pyramid) predicts rapid growth, a column predicts slow or no growth, and a narrow base predicts decline. Because young cohorts become parents, a population with a wide base keeps growing for decades even after families shrink: population momentum. Developing countries tend to have wide bases; developed countries columns or narrow bases.
total-fertility-rate: The total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime. Replacement level is about 2.1, a little above 2 because some children die young. Education and paid work for women, family planning, lower infant mortality and urban living lower TFR; where children work on farms and support parents in old age, TFR tends to stay high. A TFR below replacement means, in the long run, a shrinking population.
human-population: Crude birth and death rates count births and deaths per 1,000 people per year. Their difference divided by 10 is the rate of natural increase in percent, and 70 divided by that rate is the doubling time in years; add it to the start year to find the year a population doubles. Immigration and emigration also change population size. Malthus argued that population would outrun food; so far, food production has kept pace, but his question about limits remains.
population-transition: The demographic transition model follows a country’s crude birth and death rates as it develops. In the preindustrial stage both are high and growth is slow; in the transitional stage the death rate falls first, so growth is fastest; in the industrial stage the birth rate falls and growth slows; in the postindustrial stage both are low and the population levels off or declines. Each stage has a typical age structure diagram.
plate-tectonics: Convection in the mantle moves Earth's plates. Where plates spread apart (divergent), new crust forms; where they collide (convergent), a dense ocean plate sinks, making trenches, earthquakes and volcanoes, or continents crumple into mountains; where they slide past each other (transform), earthquakes strike. Hot spots build volcanic chains in the middle of plates. Knowing the boundary tells you the hazards a place faces.
soil-formation: Soil forms slowly from weathered parent material and humus from decomposed organisms, and it sorts into horizons: O, A (topsoil), B (subsoil), C and bedrock. Warm, wet climates form soil fastest. Wind and water erode soil, fastest where plants are removed and the ground is bare, and eroded soil harms both the land it leaves and the streams it reaches.
soil-properties: Soil texture, the share of sand, silt and clay, sets how soil behaves. Sand drains fast (high permeability) but holds little water or nutrients; clay holds water and nutrients but drains slowly; loam balances the two. The texture triangle reads a sample's class from its three percentages. Humus and a pH near 6 to 7 make soil more fertile.
atmosphere: The atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, layered by how temperature changes with height. The troposphere, heated from the ground, cools upward and holds the weather. The stratosphere warms upward because its ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet light, shielding life below. The mesosphere cools upward again, and the thin thermosphere heats sharply.
global-wind-patterns: The Sun heats the equator most, so air rises there, drops its rain, travels poleward high up and sinks near 30°, forming the Hadley cell; Ferrel and polar cells lie beyond it. Rising air brings rain and sinking air brings dry weather. Earth's rotation, the Coriolis effect, bends the surface winds into the trade winds, the westerlies and the polar easterlies.
watersheds: A watershed is all the land that drains into one stream, river or lake, bounded by high ground called a divide. Its slope, soil, plant cover and land use control how much rain runs off and how much soil and pollution reach the water. A watershed is surface land; an aquifer is water stored underground. Whatever happens anywhere in a watershed flows downstream.
solar-radiation-seasons: Insolation, the solar energy per square meter, is highest near the equator because sunlight strikes it most directly. Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so as Earth orbits, each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun: that tilt, not distance, makes the seasons. Albedo, the share of sunlight a surface reflects, decides how much of that energy the surface absorbs.
geo-and-climate: Geography reshapes climate. Mountains force moist air up, so the windward side is wet and the leeward side is a dry rain shadow. Oceans heat and cool slowly, giving coasts milder climates than inland areas. Wind-driven ocean currents carry heat: warm currents warm nearby coasts, cold currents cool them. Higher elevations are colder.
el-nino-la-nina: Normally the trade winds push warm water west across the Pacific, and cold, nutrient-rich water upwells off South America. In El Niño the trade winds weaken, warm water spreads east, upwelling weakens, fisheries off Peru decline and the rain shifts east. In La Niña the trade winds strengthen, upwelling increases and the eastern Pacific cools. This natural cycle, ENSO, shifts weather around the world.
tragedy-of-commons: A shared resource that no one controls is overused because each user gains in full from taking more while the cost is spread over everyone. Pastures, fisheries, aquifers and the atmosphere all show it. Solutions change the rewards: limits set by law, fees, assigned rights, or community rules with monitoring.
clearcutting: Clearcutting cuts every tree in an area: it is the cheapest way to harvest timber, but it bares the soil to erosion, fills streams with sediment, warms them so they hold less dissolved oxygen, washes out nutrients, and removes habitat and stored carbon. Deforestation is the lasting loss of forest to other land uses.
green-revolution: The Green Revolution greatly increased grain yields from the 1940s to the 1970s with high-yield varieties, synthetic fertilizer, irrigation, pesticides and machines. It cut hunger and spared land, but it spread monocultures with low genetic diversity, fertilizer runoff, heavy water and fossil fuel use. Genetically modified crops continue the same trade-offs.
agricultural-practices: Tilling, slash-and-burn and heavy fertilizer use each raise harvests in the short run and harm the land or water in the long run. Tilling bares the soil to erosion and loss of organic matter; slash-and-burn removes forest and releases carbon dioxide; fertilizer the crop does not use pollutes rivers, lakes and groundwater.
irrigation: Irrigation methods differ in how much of the water reaches the roots: flood and furrow are cheap but lose much of it to evaporation and runoff, spray loses less, and drip loses the least but costs the most. Overirrigation causes waterlogging and salinization, and pumping groundwater faster than it recharges depletes aquifers.
pest-control: Pesticides protect crops from insects, weeds and fungi, but they also kill nontarget organisms, run off into water, and lose their power as pests evolve resistance by natural selection. Spraying more often or switching chemicals keeps the cycle going. Genetically modified crops can cut some spraying but face the same resistance problem.
meat-production: Meat is produced in concentrated animal feeding operations, which are cheap and use little land on site but concentrate manure and depend on feed crops, or on pasture by free-range and rotational grazing, which spreads the impact but needs more land. Overgrazing strips plant cover and erodes soil and in dry regions leads to desertification. Eating lower on the food chain uses less land and feed.
overfishing: Overfishing takes fish faster than they can reproduce, so stocks shrink and can collapse, as Atlantic cod did off Newfoundland in 1992. Bycatch kills nontarget animals, and bottom trawling destroys sea-floor habitat. Catch limits, protected areas, gear rules and closed seasons are the main fixes.
mining: Mining extracts ore and coal by surface methods (strip, open-pit, mountaintop removal), which remove overburden over large areas, or by subsurface methods, which are more dangerous for miners. Waste rock and tailings release acid mine drainage and toxic metals; mining also causes erosion, sediment and dust, and clears habitat. Land reclamation restores mined land, and lower-grade ores mean more waste per kilogram of metal.
urbanization: Urbanization replaces soil and plants with impervious surfaces. Rain runs off instead of soaking in, so floods rise higher and faster, groundwater recharge falls, and runoff carries pollutants and heat to streams. Coastal pumping can cause saltwater intrusion, dark surfaces create urban heat islands, and urban sprawl spreads all of this outward.
ecological-footprints: An ecological footprint is the land and water area needed to supply a person's or population's consumption and absorb its carbon dioxide; a carbon footprint counts emissions only. Footprints rise with diet, energy use and goods, and they are far larger in wealthy countries. Footprint per person times population gives a country's total, and comparing it with biocapacity shows whether resources are used faster than they renew.
sustainability: Sustainability means meeting present needs without reducing future generations' ability to meet theirs. For a living resource such as fish or timber, the maximum sustainable yield is the largest harvest the population can replace each year, at about half its carrying capacity for logistic growth. Environmental indicators such as biodiversity, food production, carbon dioxide and temperature, population and resource depletion show whether a system is becoming more or less sustainable.
urban-runoff: Methods to reduce urban runoff let rain soak in or be held near where it falls: permeable pavement, rain gardens, green roofs, rain barrels, trees and parks, and building upward and with transit so less land is paved. They lower flood peaks, cut sewer overflows, trap pollutants and recharge groundwater, at the cost of building and upkeep.
integrated-pest-management: Integrated pest management keeps pests below damaging levels by monitoring them, preventing outbreaks, and using biological, physical and cultural controls first and targeted pesticides only when counts pass an action threshold. It cuts pesticide use, protects natural enemies, pollinators and water, and slows resistance, but it takes more knowledge, labor and time.
sustainable-agriculture: Sustainable agriculture keeps farmland productive for the long run. Contour plowing, strip cropping and terracing slow water on slopes; no-till farming and windbreaks protect the soil surface; crop rotation, legumes and perennial and cover crops protect fertility and break pest cycles; organic fertilizer adds nutrients and organic matter; and liming corrects acidic soil. Each works by slowing water or wind, or by building soil.
aquaculture: Aquaculture, raising fish and shellfish in ponds, tanks and net pens, supplies about half of the fish people eat and can ease pressure on wild stocks with high yields on little space. Open pens release concentrated waste, spread disease and parasites to wild fish, use antibiotics and lose escaped fish, and carnivorous species are fed wild fish. Closed tanks and plant-eating or filter-feeding species reduce these costs.
sustainable-forestry: Sustainable forestry harvests wood no faster than forests regrow while protecting soil, water and habitat. Selective cutting keeps most trees standing; reforestation replants cut land; prescribed burns remove fuel so wildfires stay cooler; and reusing and recycling wood lowers demand. Each method trades some cost or timber for a forest that keeps producing.
renewable-nonrenewable: Energy resources are sorted by how fast nature replaces them. Nonrenewable sources (coal, oil, natural gas, nuclear fuel) form over millions of years, so their supply is fixed. Renewable sources are replenished on a human timescale: sunlight and wind are nondepletable, while wood and other biomass are depletable and stay renewable only if they are harvested no faster than they regrow.
global-energy-consumption: The world runs mostly on fossil fuels, about 80 percent of its energy. Energy use per person is far higher in developed countries, while total use is growing fastest in developing countries as their populations and incomes rise. Reading energy data means comparing totals and per-person values with numbers, and percent change is (new - old) / old × 100.
fuel-types: The main fuels differ in energy per kilogram, carbon dioxide per unit of energy and use. Coal ranks from lignite to bituminous to anthracite as heat and pressure raise its carbon and energy content. Crude oil is refined into transportation fuels; natural gas, mostly methane, releases about half the carbon dioxide of coal for the same energy but is not zero emissions. Cogeneration puts waste heat to use.
energy-resources-distribution: Energy resources are spread unevenly because they depend on geology and climate. Fossil fuels sit in sedimentary basins where ancient organisms were buried; Earth's internal heat is near the surface at plate boundaries; sunlight, wind and falling water vary with latitude, clouds and terrain. A country without the resources it uses must import energy. Proven reserves count what can be recovered profitably now, and reserve ÷ yearly production estimates how long they last.
fossil-fuels: A fossil fuel power plant burns fuel to make steam, which spins a turbine and generator. Each step loses energy as heat, so only about a third of the fuel's energy becomes electricity; overall efficiency is the product of the step efficiencies. Fossil fuels are dense and reliable but release carbon dioxide and pollutants. Fracking has unlocked shale gas and oil, with risks to groundwater and air.
nuclear-power: Nuclear power plants split uranium-235 nuclei in a controlled chain reaction; the heat makes steam that spins a turbine, with no carbon dioxide released while running. Radioactive isotopes decay with a fixed half-life, so amount left = start × 0.5^(time ÷ half-life). The costs are a nonrenewable mined fuel, waste that must be stored for thousands of years, warm water released to rivers, and the rare but severe risk of a meltdown.
biomass-energy: Biomass energy releases the sunlight stored in wood, crops and waste, either by burning or by making biofuels such as ethanol and biodiesel. It is renewable when harvest matches regrowth, and regrowth reabsorbs the carbon dioxide released. But burning biomass pollutes the air, especially indoors, and fuel crops use land, water and fossil energy; clearing forest for them can release more carbon than the fuel saves.
solar-energy: Solar energy can be turned into electricity by photovoltaic cells or by mirrors that make steam, or used as heat through active collectors or passive building design. It releases no emissions while running and never runs out, but it is intermittent, so it needs storage or backup, and large solar farms use land and can disturb habitat. Savings are kWh times the price per kWh.
hydroelectric: Hydroelectric power turns the energy of falling water into electricity with a turbine and generator. It is renewable, emits nothing while running and can be adjusted quickly, which makes it the world's largest renewable source of electricity. But dams flood valleys, displace people, block fish migration, trap sediment and change rivers downstream. Run-of-the-river and tidal systems avoid large reservoirs but have their own limits.
geothermal: Geothermal energy is heat from Earth's interior. Where hot rock is near the surface, at plate boundaries and hot spots, wells bring up steam to spin turbines day and night, and cooled water is reinjected so the resource lasts. Ground source heat pumps move heat between buildings and the steady-temperature shallow ground almost anywhere. Limits are few good power plant sites, drilling costs, some released gases and the risk of depleting a field.
hydrogen-fuel-cell: A hydrogen fuel cell turns the chemical energy of hydrogen and oxygen into electricity without burning, and its only exhaust is water. But hydrogen is an energy carrier that must be made, mostly from natural gas today, so emissions move to where it is produced. Fuel cells refuel quickly and suit buses and trucks, but hydrogen is hard to store, fueling stations are scarce, and the chain from electricity to wheels is far less efficient than a battery.
wind-energy: Wind turbines turn the kinetic energy of moving air into electricity with blades, a gearbox and a generator. Wind is renewable, needs no fuel, releases no carbon dioxide while running and shares land with farming, so it has some of the lowest life-cycle emissions of any source. Its drawbacks are intermittency, which calls for storage or backup, harm to birds and bats, noise and views, and the need for new power lines.
energy-conservation: Energy conservation means using less energy; energy efficiency means using less for the same service. Savings are calculated by chains whose units cancel: the change in watts times hours, converted to kWh, then times the price for dollars and times the emission factor for carbon dioxide. At home, insulation, thermostats, LEDs and efficient appliances save energy; at large scale, fuel economy standards, hybrid and electric vehicles, public transportation and green building design do.
air-pollution: Air pollutants are primary (released directly: CO, NOx, SO2, particulates, VOCs) or secondary (formed in the air: ozone near the ground, sulfuric and nitric acid). Coal burning is the main source of SO2 and mercury; hot combustion makes NOx; CO starves the blood of oxygen; PM2.5 reaches deep into the lungs. The Clean Air Act sets limits on six criteria pollutants.
photochemical-smog: Photochemical smog is a mix of secondary pollutants, mainly ground-level ozone, made when nitrogen oxides and VOCs react in sunlight. NO from morning traffic becomes NO2; sunlight splits NO2, and the freed oxygen atom forms ozone, which VOCs help build up. Ozone peaks in the early afternoon on hot, sunny days, irritates lungs and damages plants, and falls after dark.
thermal-inversion: A thermal inversion is a layer of warm air over cooler air near the ground, the reverse of the normal pattern. The cool, dense air cannot rise through the warm layer, so smoke, exhaust and particles build up near the ground. Inversions form on clear, calm nights and winter mornings and in valleys and basins, and they break when the sun warms the ground or wind mixes the air.
co2-particulates: Carbon dioxide and particulate matter have natural sources as well as human ones. Volcanoes, wildfires, respiration and decomposition release CO2, though human emissions are now about 100 times volcanic ones. Volcanic ash, wildfire smoke, desert dust, sea spray and pollen add particles. Particles scatter and absorb light, causing haze, and fine particles harm the lungs whatever their source.
indoor-air: Indoor air pollutants include radon from uranium in rock, formaldehyde and other VOCs off-gassed by new materials, carbon monoxide from poorly burning stoves and furnaces, asbestos fibers from disturbed old insulation, and smoke from cooking over open fires. Tight buildings trap them. Testing, ventilation, removing the source and CO detectors reduce the harm.
reducing-air-pollutants: Air pollutants are cut by using cleaner fuel, burning it better, or capturing pollutants after burning. Scrubbers remove SO2; electrostatic precipitators and baghouse filters remove particles; catalytic converters change CO, NOx and hydrocarbons into less harmful gases; vapor recovery nozzles capture gasoline vapor. Laws such as emission caps and cap-and-trade programs make these cuts happen. None of the devices removes CO2.
acid-rain: Acid deposition forms when sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from power plants and vehicles react in the air to make sulfuric and nitric acid, which fall in rain, snow and fog or as dry particles, often far downwind. Each drop of 1 in pH is ten times more acidic. It acidifies lakes, harms fish and forests, and dissolves stone; limestone buffers it. Cutting SO2 and NOx raised rain pH.
noise-pollution: Noise pollution is sound that harms people or wildlife because of its level or timing. It is measured in decibels, a logarithmic scale where each 10 dB is 10 times the intensity, and long exposure above about 85 dB damages hearing. Noise also raises stress in people and masks the sounds animals use to mate, feed and migrate. Barriers, quieter machines, slower ships, hearing protection and rules reduce it.
pollution-sources: Point sources release pollution from one identifiable place, such as a pipe or smokestack, so they can be measured, permitted and treated. Nonpoint sources, such as runoff from farms, lawns and streets, come from many diffuse places. Laws have cut point sources sharply, so nonpoint pollution is now the largest share, and it is reduced by changing how land is used.
human-impacts-ecosystems: Pollution changes ecosystems by pushing conditions outside species' tolerance ranges. Indicator species such as mayfly larvae reveal water quality. Heat stress bleaches corals by making them expel their algae; sediment smothers reefs; oil spills coat and poison wildlife; and plastics entangle animals and break into microplastics that enter food webs.
endocrine-disruptors: Endocrine disruptors are chemicals that interfere with hormones by mimicking them, blocking their receptors or changing how much is made. Atrazine, BPA, phthalates and synthetic estrogens are examples. Even at very low doses they can cause intersex fish, abnormal frog development and human reproductive and developmental problems. Limits on use, extra cleaning steps at wastewater plants and safe medicine disposal reduce them.
wetlands-mangroves: Wetlands and mangroves provide valuable ecosystem services: they store floodwater, recharge groundwater, filter pollutants, store carbon, buffer coasts against storm surge and shelter fish and birds. Draining and filling them for development and farms, and clearing mangroves for shrimp ponds, removes these services, raising flood and storm damage and lowering water quality. Permits, mitigation and restoration protect them.
eutrophication: Cultural eutrophication happens when nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizer, manure and sewage enter water. The extra nutrients feed an algal bloom that shades plants below; when the algae and plants die, decomposers use oxygen to break them down, dissolved oxygen falls, and fish and bottom animals die in hypoxic dead zones. Keeping nutrients on the land and out of water prevents it.
thermal-pollution: Thermal pollution is heat added to water by people, mostly from power plant and factory cooling water and from warm runoff. Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen while raising the oxygen needs of fish, so cold-water species decline, and sudden changes cause thermal shock. Cooling towers and ponds, shade along streams and temperature limits reduce it.
persistent-organic-pollutants: Persistent organic pollutants are synthetic, carbon-based chemicals such as DDT, PCBs and dioxins that resist breakdown, dissolve in fat, travel long distances on wind and water and stay toxic for decades. They collect in cold regions and in animal fat, harming reproduction and development; DDT thinned the eggshells of birds of prey. Bans such as the Stockholm Convention cut new inputs, but levels fall slowly.
bioaccumulation-biomagnification: Bioaccumulation is the build-up of a persistent, fat-soluble pollutant in one organism over its life. Biomagnification is the rise in its concentration at each higher trophic level, because each consumer eats many organisms and keeps their stored pollutant. DDT, PCBs and methylmercury reach their highest levels in top predators, thinning eggshells in birds of prey and leading to fish advisories for people.
solid-waste: Municipal solid waste in the United States is mostly landfilled (about half in 2018), with the rest recycled, composted or burned. Sanitary landfills use liners, leachate collection, soil cover, gas wells and caps to contain trash; buried organic waste decomposes slowly without oxygen and makes methane. Incineration cuts volume but releases air pollutants and ash. E-waste needs special handling, and ocean dumping is banned.
waste-reduction: Waste is reduced by following the hierarchy: reduce first (less packaging, durable goods), then reuse, then recycle and compost, then recover energy, with landfilling last. Recycling saves materials and energy but has costs; composting turns food and yard waste into soil and avoids landfill methane. Policies such as pay-as-you-throw, bag fees and deposits shift behavior, and landfill gas can generate electricity.
sewage-treatment: Sewage treatment cleans wastewater in stages. Primary treatment physically removes solids as sludge; secondary treatment uses microbes in aerated tanks to break down dissolved organic matter and cut BOD; tertiary treatment removes nitrogen and phosphorus; disinfection kills germs. Sludge is digested and disposed of or reused. Septic systems treat wastewater for single homes, and combined sewers can overflow in storms.
lethal-dose-50: LD50 is the dose, in milligrams per kilogram of body mass, that kills half of a test population; it is read off a graph of percent killed against dose at the 50% line. The lower the LD50, the more toxic the substance. Multiply the LD50 by a body mass to get a whole-body dose, writing the units so kilograms cancel, and convert milligrams to grams when asked.
dose-response-curve: A dose-response curve shows the percent of a test group responding at each dose. It is flat at zero below the threshold dose, rises steeply through 50% and levels off near 100%. Read across from 50% and down to find the LD50 (deaths) or ED50 (another effect). The substance whose curve rises at lower doses is more toxic, and harm can begin far below the LD50.
pollution-human-health: Linking a pollutant to a disease is hard because people face many exposures over long times. Synergism means pollutants together can do more harm than their effects added. Acute effects follow short, high exposures; chronic effects follow long ones. Know ground-level ozone and lung function, asbestos and mesothelioma, and sewage-contaminated water and dysentery.
pathogens: Pathogens are bacteria, viruses, protozoa, fungi and worms that cause infectious diseases. They spread through water, air, food, contact and vectors such as mosquitoes and fleas. Poor sanitation and crowding speed the spread, which is why clean water and sewage treatment prevent cholera. A warming climate can widen the range of vectors and the diseases they carry.
ozone-depletion: The stratospheric ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun’s UV. CFCs drift up to the stratosphere, where UV frees chlorine, and each chlorine atom destroys many thousands of ozone molecules because it is released again after each cycle. The ozone hole forms over Antarctica each spring. Thinner ozone lets more UV-B through, raising skin cancer and cataracts. Carbon dioxide is not an ozone-depleting gas.
reducing-ozone-depletion: The Montreal Protocol of 1987 phased out CFCs, halons and other ozone-depleting substances worldwide. HCFCs were a stopgap that still contains chlorine; HFCs spare ozone but trap heat, so the Kigali Amendment phases them down. Hydrocarbon and other refrigerants and capture of old refrigerant help too. Ozone is recovering slowly because CFCs last for decades.
greenhouse-effect: Sunlight warms the surface, which gives off infrared; greenhouse gases (water vapor, CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide, CFCs) absorb it and send part back down, keeping Earth about 33 °C warmer. More gas traps more heat. Global warming potential compares gases with CO₂: multiply a mass by its GWP for CO₂ equivalent. The greenhouse effect is not ozone depletion.
greenhouse-gas-increases: Burning fossil fuels and clearing forests add CO₂; livestock, rice paddies, landfills and gas leaks add methane; fertilizer adds nitrous oxide. The Keeling curve shows CO₂ at Mauna Loa rising from about 317 ppm in 1960 to over 420 ppm, faster each decade. Ice cores show it stayed between about 180 and 300 ppm for 800,000 years.
climate-change: More greenhouse gases warm Earth. Warming melts land ice, which raises sea level, and melts sea ice, which does not raise sea level but lowers albedo. Positive feedback loops such as melting ice and thawing permafrost amplify warming. Effects include heat waves, droughts, heavy rain, coastal flooding and species shifting toward the poles.
ocean-warming: The ocean absorbs about 90% of the extra heat. Warmer water expands (thermal expansion), which with melting land ice raises sea level. Warm water holds less oxygen and mixes less, so oxygen and surface nutrients fall. Heat stress bleaches corals and pushes species toward the poles. The thermohaline circulation, driven by temperature and salinity, could slow as fresh meltwater enters the North Atlantic.
ocean-acidification: The ocean absorbs part of the CO₂ people add to the air. Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions and lowers pH; those ions also bind carbonate, so corals, oysters and some plankton struggle to build calcium carbonate. pH has fallen from about 8.2 to 8.1; because the scale is logarithmic, that is about 26% more hydrogen ions. Cutting CO₂ emissions is the fix.
invasive-species: Invasive species are nonnative species that spread quickly and cause harm. They are often generalists with r-selected traits that face few predators in their new home. They outcompete natives and are very hard to remove once established. Zebra mussels, kudzu and cane toads are classic cases. Prevention, such as ballast water rules and boat cleaning, and early detection are the best tools.
endangered-species: Endangered species face extinction now; threatened species likely will soon. Specialists, K-selected species, small populations and species that need large territories are most at risk. The US Endangered Species Act protects listed species and their critical habitat, and CITES controls international trade. Recovery works when the cause of decline is removed, as with the bald eagle after DDT was banned.
human-impacts-biodiversity: Human impacts on biodiversity are summed up as HIPPCO: habitat loss (the leading cause), invasive species, pollution, human population growth, climate change and overexploitation. Fragmentation leaves small, isolated populations that are easily lost. Today’s extinction rate may mark a sixth mass extinction. Protected areas, wildlife corridors, catch limits and restoration help reverse the losses.
